data.title: Meet the home buyers totally unfazed by 7% mortgage rates
data.description:
By Aarthi Swaminathan

Individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 1 in 5 home purchases in September - the highest share in a little over a year

While mortgage rates over 7% have everyday house hunters pulling back from the market, data suggest that real-estate investors are sticking it out.

In June, real-estate investor Justin Smith closed on a duplex in Roscoe, Ill. - about 90 miles west of Chicago - for $250,000. The rate on his 30-year fixed mortgage was 7%.

Smith, a 34-year-old real-estate broker who also owns three apartment buildings in Roscoe and nearby Rockford, told MarketWatch that smaller Midwestern cities in particular offer an easy way into real-estate investing, because the barrier to entry - namely, home prices - is relatively low. The average home value in Rockford, Ill., is about $185,000, according to Zillow's (Z) (ZG) estimates, compared to a national median value of about $366,000.

More importantly, "we have such a strong rental population," Smith said, meaning that many people in the area rent instead of own.

Smith isn't the only real-estate investor who's buying right now. While surging mortgage rates over 7% have everyday house hunters pulling back from the market, data suggest that real-estate investors are sticking it out.

In September, individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 20% of home-purchase transactions - the highest share in a little over a year, according to the National Association of Realtors.

"Investors tend to pull back less than noninvestor buyers when conditions deteriorate," Hannah Jones, a senior economist at Realtor.com, told MarketWatch. "So their share of total buyers rises as higher mortgage rates squeeze out more noninvestor buyers." (Realtor.com is operated by News Corp subsidiary Move Inc.; MarketWatch publisher Dow Jones is also a subsidiary of News Corp.)

"There are opportunities for investors today that we haven't seen in years. Inventory is rising, sellers are cutting prices and negotiating leverage is shifting toward buyers," Michael Carbonare, another real-estate investor, told MarketWatch.

In September, the total for-sale housing inventory in the U.S. jumped to 1.6 million units, the highest level since November 2019, NAR said. About 43% of sellers were cutting prices as of Oct. 12, according to separate data from ParclHQ.

"It's a good time to be looking for motivated sellers, buying right and structuring deals that make financial sense," Carbonare said.

Related: U.S. wealth has shifted to stocks from homes. There are big reasons to worry.

Relatively small-time real-estate investors - those who own three to nine properties - have been more active than large landlords. About 14.5% of home purchases made in August were by smaller real-estate investors, which was up from 13.6% a year ago, according to Cotality, a real-estate data-analytics company.

In contrast, 9% of purchases were by medium-sized investors, and 2% were by large investors.

One factor driving some investors to buy houses now is strong rental demand. Rents nationally are trending upwards: In September, the typical rent rose 2.7% from the same time a year ago to around $1,900, Zillow found in an analysis.

"Elevated mortgage rates have pushed home shoppers straight into the arms of rentals," Kara Ng, a senior economist at Zillow, said in the report.

The company estimated that demand for single-family rentals rose nearly 22% in September from the previous year, and 10% for multifamily or apartment rentals.

In Chicago, where the typical rent grew 4.7% in September from last year to about $2,200, according to Zillow, 66-year-old Tom Moran is putting down $500,000 for a $2 million, six-unit apartment building in the city - the latest addition to his portfolio of 18 other buildings.

The mortgage rate was 6.625% for the bank-portfolio loan Moran used to finance the purchase, though he said the rate wasn't a concern for him. "It's just a number," Moran, a real-estate investor and broker who is now under contract on the property, told MarketWatch.

"Interest rates go up, interest rates go down - but in general, real estate is a long-term buy," he said. "I look at real estate as basically like a little business ... so I'm not worried about the initial return."

Having bought his first property in the late 1980s when the 30-year mortgage rate averaged over 10%, Moran said he's accustomed to high-rate environments.

As part of his due diligence before his latest purchase, Moran called up a few mortgage lenders for quotes before he pulled the trigger. The rates he was quoted ranged from mid-6% to over 7% - but he said he was unfazed.

"People freak out" when they see the 7% handle, Moran noted. On the loan he was pursuing, the rate going up a quarter point, from 6.875% to 7.125%, amounted to a roughly $250 hit per month for him. "It's not a deal-breaker," he said.

Do you have questions about real estate and home-buying that you would like to see covered in MarketWatch? We'd love to hear from you. You can write to us at readerstories@marketwatch.com. A reporter may be in touch to learn more. MarketWatch will not attribute your answers to you by name without your permission.

-Aarthi Swaminathan

data.title: 'Some people did everything right': I lost my home in the Great Recession. I rent in my 50s. Why is that judged as failure?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I earn $110,000 a year'

"Saving for a down payment is not easy in a major metropolitan area when a house costs three to four times your annual income." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I read the letter about mortgage applications and your response (As a mortgage loan officer, I rejected wealthy couples. Here's what can get your application declined.), and I agree with much of what this reader says. Living within your means, avoiding (unnecessary) debt and saving are good advice. There's a lot to be said for the discipline of "Joe Six-Pack," as the mortgage loan officer described him, who earns less but saves and eventually buys a home.

But there's another side of this that often gets overlooked - which, in fairness, you did address somewhat in your answer. I'm in my 50s, and the Great Recession hit at the worst time in my life. I wasn't a fool, but I did try to build a life for myself by buying a house. Still, the housing crash had consequences that lasted far longer than the recession itself. I lost my job and eventually my home. I earn $110,000 a year and it's still hard.

For people my age, getting knocked off the property ladder can be very hard to recover from. Those who already owned a home and held on to it through the downturn benefited enormously from the rise in property values that followed. Those who lost a home, sold at the wrong time or couldn't buy during those years missed out on that appreciation entirely. It was a matter of timing for many people, not reckless abandon as the mortgage loan officer would like us to believe.

Some people did everything right and were caught on the wrong side of an economic shock. Let me also tell you that saving for a down payment is not easy in a major metropolitan area when a house costs three to four times your annual income. So my message to your letter writer is to be careful about turning a lesson in spending too much into a judgment of people who haven't hit the same milestones. I am happy for friends and family who have homes, but it still stings.

Why judge other people for not getting on the property ladder?

Renter in His 50s

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: I'm 77, pay rent and live off Social Security, but I help homeless people. Why are so many people going hungry?

Homeownership in the U.S. has averaged 61% in Gallup polls since 2012, down from 70% between 2001 and 2011.

Dear Renter,

We are all on our own paths, and I'd bet that people who judge others for having less are insecure around those who have more.

You did not come out of the 2008-09 recession unscathed, and I can see why it rankles when somebody in a position of authority, even power, talks critically about would-be homebuyers putting too much money on credit cards or not saving enough of their salary, even though they earn a six-figure income. You have a right to feel the way you do, and you furthermore have a right to express it. I'm glad you chose to do that here.

For the record, the mortgage loan officer in question struck me as alarmist and at times judgmental. "People in the U.S. need to wake up and not be compulsive," she wrote. "Quit buying things you really don't need. It's that way with the federal government as well, and based on that, we'd better get real quick or we're going to have a financial crisis that makes the Great Recession of 2008 look like a picnic."

It's painful to have had a home once upon a time only to lose it, and to realize how much you lost. It was, sad to say, not an uncommon story during the last recession, when the unemployment rate rose to 10% and the number of foreclosure filings hit 2.8 million in 2009. I believe it helps enormously to know that this was a shared, collective trauma, and that many millions of people around the world also went through what you experienced.

Many millions of people around the world went through what you experienced.

High interest rates - the 30-year mortgage rate hit 7.3% in early October, nearly three times its level five years ago - and high house prices mean that buying a home remains out of reach for people who no longer have home equity to leverage, as well as for many first-time buyers. There's also a dearth of inventory in many markets, which has led to a generation of renters in their 30s, 40s, 50s and beyond. It can be a bitter pill to swallow.

At $110,000 a year, or $9,200 a month before taxes, lenders prefer housing costs at or below 30% of gross income. If you took a mortgage rate of 7.3%, even with money set aside for property taxes and insurance, you could afford a $300,000 property. That amount would be further reduced by student debt, a car payment and/or credit-card debt. And that's before you pull the money together for a down payment.

You would need to drum up $90,000 for a 20% down payment. That makes your task even more challenging after a job loss or foreclosure. Location matters too, as you say you live in a major metropolitan area. In the Midwest and South, $110,000 could buy a decent home, but in the New York, Boston, Los Angeles or Seattle areas, median prices can top $800,000, depending on the neighborhood.

Related: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Homeownership rates have fallen

A recent Gallup poll shed light on what you are experiencing, and the results did not bode well for a generation of renters who would like to get their foot on the property ladder. The share of U.S. non-homeowners who expect to buy a home within five years has dropped to 25%, the lowest level Gallup has recorded since it began asking the question more than a decade ago. The poll found that 61% of Americans say they own their primary residence, while 34% rent.

Homeownership in the U.S. has averaged 61% in Gallup polls since 2012. Some 28% of non-homeowners told Gallup that they expect to buy a home within 10 years and just 25% said they expect to do so within five years, while 45% do not think they will do so at all in the foreseeable future. More worryingly, all of those figures have dropped over the past 10 years.

My colleagues Jillian Berman and Venessa Wong recently wrote about young Americans who feel shut out of the housing market - seemingly forever, in some cases. As they pointed out, the median age of renters in America now hovers around 42, up from 38 in 2006, and nearly one-third of renters have a college degree or higher, compared with 22% in 2010, according to Census Bureau data. Meanwhile, the national average rent is now $1,665 per month.

Renters are getting older, even if younger adults make up the largest share.

There has been some good news for renters. A 2026 report on rental housing from Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies said that after record-high increases during the pandemic, national rent growth has stayed near zero since mid-2023. Most markets experienced either small declines or small increases. In 74 of the largest 150 markets, asking rents fell, while 70 recorded modest growth of less than 4%. Rents rose by 4% or more in only six markets.

Perhaps the most significant takeaway is that renters are getting older, even if younger adults still make up the largest share of the renting population. Although there were roughly 6.1 million renters in your age group (50-59) in 2024, that number is down from 6.7 million in 2014. But there were more renters ages 60 to 69 (5.4 million versus 4.4 million in 2014) and 70 to 79 (3.4 million versus 2.3 million). That is a mixed picture at best.

Some 13% of renters are in their 50s, based on the most recent data from the U.S. Census Bureau. Adding up all those people from the JCHS report, 10.9 million people ages 60 and over are renters. That affects their financial security now and when they retire. Housing remains the biggest monthly expense for most people, and having to pay rent in your 60s does not make retirement any easier. Keep on saving and planning.

Take a bow. You are a survivor and, given the kind of upheaval you have endured, you are living a different kind of American dream.

Related: I'm 71 and still working. I earn $108,000 a year. Am I doing the right thing?

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns or email The Moneyist on qfottrell@marketwatch.com.

My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

'I'm never selling': I'm 47 and buy bitcoin with every dollar I earn. Am I crazy?

'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

On May 28, 2026, before the market opened, Morpheus Research published a report alleging that Innventure's DarkNX venture to build an AI data center campus in Ontario was a fabrication. The report revealed there was "zero evidence this project exists or that DarkNX has the team or funding to even contemplate such a project." Morpheus Research further reported that "[a]ccording to a former Innventure executive, management was using 'false information' and revenue projections that were 'pure fiction' to solicit investments into Accelsius." The report quoted multiple former Accelsius employees, who stated, among other things, "we've never heard of the company [DarkNX], they don't have customers, there's no data center."

On this news, Innventure's stock price fell $0.54 per share, or 8.42%, to close at $5.87 per share on May 28, 2026, on unusually heavy trading volume.

On August 13, 2026, after the market closed, Innventure reported second quarter 2026 results. Among other items, Innventure disclosed a net loss of $34.9 million, compared to $27.8 million in the first quarter of 2026, and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $22.6 million, compared to $18.4 million in the first quarter of 2026. The Company also announced it is "suspending [its] previously communicated expectations regarding Accelsius' 2026 revenue and cash flow targets and shifting [its] focus."

On the same day, Innventure filed its quarterly report on Form 10-Q with the SEC, disclosing that "the deployment site identified in the DarkNX purchase order is no longer available. Accelsius has removed the DarkNX project from its internal bookings."

On this news, Innventure's stock price fell $1.98 per share, or 55%, to close at $1.62 per share on August 14, 2026, on unusually heavy trading volume.

data.title: Silver's recent 50% drop from a record high hints that an economic slowdown looms
data.description:
By Myra P. Saefong

Silver is more 'economically sensitive' than gold, notes one precious-metals dealer

Silver's price action may offer hints on the economy amid inflation driven by rising fuel prices.

There's a relatively off-the-radar commodity that can provide hints on where the economy is headed - and it's seen its value drop more than 50% from a record high earlier this year.

"Silver is more economically sensitive than gold, so its recent price weakness may be a leading indicator of underlying issues in the broader economy," said Stefan Gleason, president and CEO at Money Metals Exchange.

Silver can be seen as hybrid leading indicator because of its dual role as a monetary precious metal and an industrial commodity. Prices for silver (SIZ26) (SI00) reached a record intraday high of $121.79 an ounce in late January, according to Dow Jones Market Data - but have since dropped more than 50% to end at $57.31 an ounce Friday.

Gold (GCZ26) (GC00) has dropped too, but nowhere near as much as silver. The yellow metal has lost over 25% from its record high of $5,626.80 an ounce in January.

Silver's decline "syncs up with the warning lights we are seeing in the energy markets - with persistently high energy prices virtually certain to slow the economy, or worse," Gleason told MarketWatch.

Year to date, U.S. and global benchmark prices for crude oil (CL.1) (BRN00) have climbed by more than 70%, in large part due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East that has disrupted production and shipments of the commodity. In a sign of the rising cost of refined oil, the price of diesel at the pump has spiked nearly 78% since the end of last year to stand at $6.30 a gallon Friday, according to GasBuddy.

Those increases were evident in the latest U.S. inflation data, which showed hotter prices than the market expected. The consumer-price index rose 0.6% in September and gained 3.7% year over year, while the producer-price index was up 1.3% last month and climbed 6.3% year over year.

Silver, meanwhile, is "reflecting some of the economic headwinds higher inflation is causing in the global economy," said Dana Samuelson, president of American Gold Exchange.

He explained that gold and silver are, for most people, discretionary purchases - in other words, more of a want rather than a need. And when inflation erodes spending power, those discretionary purchases slow, Samuelson noted.

For now, it's tough to measure just how much the inflationary impulse of a roughly doubling of the diesel price in the last six months has had on the global economy, but the market could be starting to see the "first ripple of that inflationary impulse," he said.

"That may be what the declining silver price is telling us now, because silver's value is approximately 50% monetary and 50% commodity," said Samuelson. Gold has seen a smaller decline from record highs, but it's more of a precious metal - 90% monetary and 10% commodity, he said.

Silver is also more subject to investor sentiment than gold, said Robert Minter, director of ETF investment strategy at Aberdeen Investments.

Global central-bank purchases of gold were a key reason why prices for the metal reached a record high earlier this year, and central-bank purchases are a "strategic source" of demand for the yellow metal, said Minter. "That same-size strategic buyer does not exist for silver," he added, making it more sensitive to investor sentiment.

Silver's outsize selloff

It's true, however, that it's not unusual for silver prices to move a lot more than gold prices.

Silver's sharper price decline than gold reflects its "greater volatility, exposure to industrial demand, and the unwinding of earlier speculative enthusiasm," said Ryan McIntyre, president of Sprott.

Earlier this year, as prices for gold were on track to notch record highs, some traders looked for a cheaper and quicker way to participate in that rise, leading to what can be referred to as speculative enthusiasm in the market.

But volatility often accompanies large and quick moves, and that's particularly true when "turbulence hits major markets, causing liquidity-driven selloffs" like the one seen earlier this week, Samuelson said.

On Wednesday, silver for December delivery, the most active futures contract, fell 6.1%, the largest one-day drop since June 24, and settled at $55.88 an ounce, the lowest since Nov. 26, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Gold that day posted a modest decline of 1.7%.

Higher inflation readings are not surprising given high energy prices, but they still "spooked equity markets" Wednesday, said Samuelson. And when that happens, gold and silver prices can "temporarily suffer as a casualty of those selloffs," he said.

Once the dust settles from these market selloffs, gold and silver prices often rebound quickly due to bargain buying, Samuelson said.

Prices for both metals ended higher Thursday, even after producer-price index data also showed a bigger-than-expected rise. Silver rose slightly again on Friday, but was still down more than 6% on the week.

Looking further ahead, silver still has potential to find support from stronger demand, stemming from growth in artificial intelligence and the data-center build-out.

"Investment across smart-grid infrastructure and data transmission supports silver demand, and we see AI as a growth source for the next several years," said Trevor Yates, senior investment analyst at Global X ETFs. Silver's "increasing industrial utility" underpins the metal's growing physical scarcity, he noted, with the physical-market forecast to remain in deficit for the sixth straight year in 2026.

While silver could stay volatile in the short term, Yates said Global X ETFs increasingly sees precious metals as an "interesting opportunity" for 2027.

-Myra P. Saefong

data.title: Influencers and biohackers swear by fasting. Here's what the science says.
data.description:
By Beth Krietsch

Fasting can help some people reduce how many calories they eat - but it's not 'effortless' as some would have you believe

Intermittent fasting can help people lose weight - but the research behind purported benefits, like improvements in cognitive health, is sparse.

About 15% of Americans followed an intermittent-fasting diet last year, thanks in part to a push from biohackers and health influencers confidently touting it as the key to effortless weight loss.

But when you dig into the scientific research, the findings are more nuanced.

Intermittent fasting is a way of eating whereby you only consume food during certain windows of time. Among American consumers, it was more popular than eating low-carb or Mediterranean diets, according to a recent survey.

There are many different approaches to intermittent fasting. With the 16:8 method, you eat during an 8-hour block of time each day and fast for the remaining 16. There's also the 5:2 diet, which involves eating normally five days out of the week, and consuming just 25% of your normal caloric intake the other two days. That often looks like having just one 500- or 600-calorie meal each day.

The general idea is that going long stretches without eating depletes the body's stored sugar, or glycogen, so it burns stored fat for energy. But it's not clear that that's what drives weight loss; a simpler explanation is that some people simply find they have an easier time cutting back on calories - like that pesky snacking habit you can't seem to shut down, no matter how hard you try - when they can only eat during specific windows of time.

Does this approach actually help with weight loss? And does it work better than other approaches? The research suggests it can lead to modest weight loss, but studies generally find it doesn't work any better than normal calorie restriction.

And influencers' claims that intermittent fasting is an "effortless" solution to weight loss are overhyped - most people probably would not consider 16 hours without eating to be "effortless" or easy.

The science behind intermittent fasting

A 2024 review found that intermittent fasting may be associated with small reductions in waist circumference and fat mass in people who are overweight or obese. And a 2025 review of 99 randomized clinical trials found that intermittent fasting is associated with modest weight loss compared to a normal, unrestricted diet.

But aside from some studies that saw some weight-loss benefits with alternate day fasting for short amounts of time, fasting generally didn't lead to any greater weight loss than traditional calorie restriction, which aligns with other research.

Similarly, in a smaller review of 22 randomized clinical trials conducted around the world, researchers concluded that for people who are overweight or obese, intermittent fasting makes little to no meaningful difference in weight loss compared to following standard dietary advice, such as cutting back on calories or eating different foods. The study's lead author even went so far as to say that the existing evidence for intermittent fasting doesn't justify the hype seen on social media.

Want to read more more first-person articles like this? Check out Health Equity, a MarketWatch column about your health

Beyond weight loss, intermittent fasting is often held up as a path to better health - from sharper mental clarity and improved insulin sensitivity to a longer life and cellular repair. Some early evidence may support a few of these claims. Research suggests that intermittent fasting may improve blood-sugar control in people with Type 2 diabetes. And while intermittent fasting isn't going to cure cancer, as some have suggested, a small study of women with advanced breast cancer found that incorporating fasting alongside resistance training during chemotherapy may be associated with slower cancer progression - though the researchers said more studies are needed.

But research showing cognitive benefits in humans is sparse, as is that on cell repair and longevity - a category that's particularly hard to study anyway. Animal studies make up a good portion of this kind of research, and without more high-quality studies in people, we can't say whether the findings translate to humans.

None of this means intermittent fasting is useless. If sticking to a clear, defined eating window helps you rein in late-night snacking, cut back on calories and stick to a nutritious diet over a long period of time, intermittent fasting may be a reasonable approach to managing your weight.

But for many Americans, it may be best approached with a healthy dose of skepticism. And for people with certain medical histories, like having an eating disorder, being pregnant or taking a SGLT2 inhibitor, fasting isn't a good idea.

Based on the evidence we have, intermittent fasting isn't superior to calorie counting for weight loss, and many claims about longevity and health optimization are far ahead of existing research evidence. It may be a useful tool for some people - but it isn't a magic wand for improving your health.

-Beth Krietsch

data.title: Microsoft, Shopify and 3 more AI stocks that are favorite Wall Street earnings plays
data.description:
By Christine Ji

As earnings season kicks off, select tech companies have the opportunity to deliver big positive surprises for investors

Surging demand for autonomous AI agents is emerging as a fresh catalyst across the tech sector.

After a tumultuous week for tech stocks, the artificial-intelligence trade faces another test as companies begin reporting their third-quarter results in earnest next week.

Concerns about whether AI can live up to the hype, combined with rising inflation, have led the Nasdaq Composite Index COMP to decline 6% from recent highs. Adding more uncertainty to the mix is Anthropic, the creator of the Claude chatbot and one of the leading AI labs. Investors are placing increased scrutiny on the company's upcoming public offering as financial concerns and AI safety risks emerge.

But earnings season can drive dramatic stock moves in a short period of time, and analysts see opportunities across select tech names that are benefiting from AI - from major cloud providers to specialized software companies.

One is Cadence Design Systems (CDNS), which has gotten caught up in the recent tech selloff, with shares falling 10% this past week. The company's core Electronic Design Automation offering is used by semiconductor companies to design and test chips.

KeyBanc analyst Jason Celino anticipates "quite a large estimate revision" when the company reports on Oct. 26, meaning that earnings expectations could zoom higher in the wake of Cadence's commentary. He cited strong demand for key products as well as fourth-quarter Wall Street expectations that look overly conservative against the company's organic revenue-growth rate, which is in the high teens.

Cadence could also be a major beneficiary of agentic opportunities, Celino told MarketWatch. As competition in the chip space heats up and design timelines compress, companies will need to supplement their design capacity with AI agents, resulting in greater usage of Cadence's platform, Celino said.

On the consumer side, the popularity of AI agents like Meta's (META) Muse assistant could provide some application software stocks with fresh catalysts heading into third-quarter earnings, according to Stifel analyst J. Parker Lane.

Lane identified Shopify (SHOP) and Twilio (TWLO) as the two biggest beneficiaries, and he expects both companies to beat earnings expectations.

As more transactions are carried out by AI assistants on behalf of shoppers, the e-commerce platform Shopify has has become "a real thought leader around agentic commerce," Lane told MarketWatch. While Amazon.com (AMZN) has blocked Muse on the platform, Shopify has opted to allow seamless agentic checkout across its stores.

Although he believes it's too early for the impact of Muse to show up this quarter, he said, Lane anticipates that Shopify's revenue growth will accelerate to 35%, beating the company's "low-thirties" forecast, thanks to strength in the company's enterprise, international and payments businesses. The company reports earnings on Nov. 3.

Lane described the cloud communications platform Twilio - which allows businesses to add voice, text, chat and other features to their software -as a neutral aggregator of the agent boom. Shares of Twilio have soared 72% since the beginning of the year, which sets a high bar going into earnings, but Lane believes the buildout and scaling of voice agents will be a key tailwind, he said.

No matter which AI agent gains the most market share, automated assistants sending text messages and placing calls will lead to a surge in overall customer communications, and businesses could lean on Twilio to manage that. Lane said he expects management to provide further details on that early AI momentum during the company's Oct. 29 earnings call.

Among the largest tech names, Jefferies analyst Brent Thill favors Microsoft (MSFT), which reports on Oct. 28. Last quarter the company posted an earnings beat driven by expanding Copilot adoption and cloud growth on its Azure platform, and Thill believes Microsoft can keep the momentum going, he said.

In a Wednesday note, Thill wrote that sustained demand for compute, or AI processing power, is allowing Microsoft to charge higher prices. Increased data-center capacity should help Azure pick up its rate of revenue growth.

To support Azure growth, Microsoft plans to spend $175 billion on infrastructure investments in 2026. Thill said he anticipates that the company could announce even higher spending levels in 2027, given the severe supply-demand imbalance for compute.

Microsoft is currently trading at a multiple of 26 times estimated forward earnings, which Thill described as "favorable" compared with a five-year average of 28.

And analysts see room for CoreWeave (CRWV) to become a turnaround play after shares of the specialized cloud-computing company fell more than 26% this week. As of June the company carried nearly $52 billion of total debt, including lease obligations. Concerns that rising interest rates will increase CoreWeave's cost of capital led yields on some of the company's unsecured debt to reach 15%, crossing into distressed territory.

In a Thursday note, Thill called the market's reaction "too harsh and not reflective of fundamentals." He pointed out that while higher rates on future deals could be a risk, CoreWeave's existing debt remain unchanged. And surging demand for AI processing power is allowing CoreWeave to charge much higher rates, more than making up the difference from higher financing costs. Thill reiterated his buy rating and $150 share-price target, which is more than 140% above current levels.

BNP Paribas analyst Daniel Wang also took an optimistic view of CoreWeave in a Thursday note, arguing that as newer, higher-priced contracts take effect across its active data centers, the leftover cash will eventually be enough to fund future infrastructure expansion.

For CoreWeave's upcoming third-quarter earnings call, Wang is looking for further details on the company's roadmap to self-sufficiency, specifically regarding how and when the company can generate enough cash flow to manage its debt obligations without relying on external funds.

-Christine Ji
